question: On smooth strongly convex quadratics, what do exact and approximate polar-factor updates reveal about Muon's minimizer reachability, time to a small loss, dependence on Hessian spectrum beyond condition number, and the reliability of one-step comparisons with gradient descent?

key_findings.claim: A constant-step exact-polar update can fail to converge even on the isotropic strongly convex quadratic, because every singular value is trapped on an initialization-dependent lattice and generically enters a two-cycle around zero.
key_findings.evidence: For L(W)=one-half times the squared Frobenius norm and W0=US0V-transpose, the update keeps U and V fixed and gives s(t+1,i)=s(t,i)-α sign(s(t,i)). Thus s(t,i) remains in s(0,i)+αZ; unless every initial singular value is aligned with αZ, the iterates miss sufficiently small loss balls.

anchors.section: 3.1, one-dimensional sign-GD and grid confinement, Equation 5

key_findings.claim: Muon-style momentum applied before projection does not remove the fixed-step lattice obstruction; momentum applied after projection can leave the lattice, but that is a different optimizer and is not Muon's default.
key_findings.evidence: Both standard and Nesterov-style pre-projection momentum still produce projected scalar directions in {−1,+1}, so every displacement is ±η. Appendix B contrasts this with Orthogonal-SGDM, whose post-projection momentum is not grid-confined but was reported in prior work to underperform a tuned SGD-momentum baseline.

anchors.section: 3.1, Momentum does not break grid confinement

key_findings.claim: The usual fixed-step stationarity guarantee contains exactly the nonvanishing residual expected from the grid trap.
key_findings.evidence: For a c-smooth loss and exact polar updates, Appendix C derives min over t<T of the nuclear norm of the gradient at most (L(W0)-L*)/(Tα)+cdα/2. The first term vanishes with T but the second is O(α); under a Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality this implies an O(α²) loss floor, matching the isotropic example.

anchors.section: Appendix C, Simple Stationarity Result, Equations 15-17

key_findings.claim: The paper's O(1/square-root-of-ε) fixed-step time-to-loss statement is a generic or worst-case scaling, not a universal lower bound for every initialization and step size.
key_findings.evidence: The argument chooses α=O(square-root-of-ε) so that the eventual two-cycle has loss O(ε), then needs Θ(1/α) steps. Yet the same scalar recurrence reaches zero exactly when s0 is an integer multiple of α, and on the isotropic matrix problem GD with step 1 reaches the optimum in one step. The authors themselves condition the discussion on ignoring reachability through a lucky initialization or asking for approach to an ε-scale neighborhood.

anchors.section: 3.2, Best possible ε-dependence under fixed steps
3.2, cycling-time calculation and contrast with GD

key_findings.claim: At a fixed Hessian condition number of 10,000, spectrum shape alone flips whether exact-projection Muon or GD wins within 500 iterations.
key_findings.evidence: The seven 100-dimensional least-squares Hessians all have eigenvalue endpoints 0.001 and 10. Across 100 Gaussian initializations and separately oracle-selected learning rates, Table 1 gives Muon win rates at T of 1 for min-spiked, U-shaped, and geometric-decay-to-max spectra, but 0 for max-spiked, uniform, Gaussian, and linear-decay-to-max spectra.

anchors.section: Appendix D.1-D.2, controlled spectra and tuning protocol

key_findings.claim: The spectrum-dependent ranking differences are often large, but the most dramatic reported Muon advantage is also the least precisely estimated.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 reports final best-GD-loss divided by best-Muon-loss of 949±620 for min-spiked, 78.0±0.3 for geometric-decay-to-max, and 2.48±0.018 for U-shaped; ratios are 0.02 or below for four unfavorable families. The 949 ratio therefore has very large uncertainty relative to its mean despite a 100-run average.

key_findings.claim: Cosine-annealed steps, Nesterov-style momentum, and Newton-Schulz projection do not erase the controlled-spectrum ranking within the reported budget, although one borderline spectrum changes quantitatively.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.6 says vanishing steps break grid confinement only late, usually after GD has converged. Tables 4-7 retain win rates 1 for min-spiked, U-shaped, and geometric-decay-to-max and 0 for most other families; linear-decay-to-max reaches only 0.03, 0.05, or 0.31 at T depending on variant.

anchors.section: Appendix D.6, Sample trajectories and robustness checks

key_findings.claim: Neither Hessian condition number nor a simple gradient-condition-number trajectory predicts the relative winner on these quadratics.
key_findings.evidence: Geometric-decay-to-max and uniform spectra both show GD gradient conditioning decreasing from roughly 100 million to 10 million, yet only the geometric family favors Muon. The loss ordering remains different despite comparable conditioning profiles.

key_findings.claim: Any nonzero Gaussian perturbation of the scalar sign update restores eventual access to every fixed neighborhood of zero almost surely.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition E.1 proves that w(n+1)=w(n)-α[sign(w(n))+σξ(n+1)] has finite hitting time of [−ε,ε] almost surely for every initialization when σ>0, whereas σ=0 never hits if the initialization lattice misses the interval. The proof combines a negative drift outside a compact set with uniformly positive bounded-length attempts inside it.

key_findings.claim: The appendix proves that both vanishingly small and arbitrarily large perturbations have poor finite-horizon hitting probabilities, but it does not prove that every instance has a unique or even strict intermediate optimum in expected or median time.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition E.2 states that for any fixed integer N, P(Tε(σ)>N) tends to 1 as σ tends to 0 or infinity when the deterministic grid misses by a positive margin. This is an extreme-limit probability statement; the intermediate 'sweet spot' is supplied by one simulation, not by an existence or uniqueness theorem for an optimizer of a hitting-time functional.

anchors.section: Appendix E.2, large-noise proof and F.1 simulation

key_findings.claim: The one-dimensional experiment exhibits a nonmonotone median hitting time under a deliberately unreachable deterministic initialization.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 and Appendix F.1 use α=0.1, ε=α/5=0.02, s0=10α+1.3ε=1.026, σ from 0.001 to 10, 10,000 independent trajectories, and a 1,000-step cap. The median and central 95% interval show an intermediate perturbation range reaching the target sooner than either extreme.

key_findings.claim: Actual Newton-Schulz approximation is not uniformly beneficial: at the final budget it helps on two of seven spectrum families by win rate and hurts on the other five.
key_findings.evidence: Against exact projection with no momentum, Table 2 gives final Newton-Schulz win rates 0.92 for max-spiked and 0.94 for min-spiked, but 0 for uniform, Gaussian, linear-decay-to-max, U-shaped, and geometric-decay-to-max. Thus the empirical evidence directly rejects a universal 'approximation helps' reading.

anchors.section: 4.3, Quadratic evidence with actual Newton-Schulz projection

key_findings.claim: Where Newton-Schulz helps most it can do so by a large best-loss factor, but its final losses are worse than exact projection on five families.
key_findings.evidence: Table 8 reports exact-loss divided by Newton-Schulz-loss at T of 33.18±8.96 for min-spiked and 1.15±0.021 for max-spiked; all other final ratios lie between 0.71 and 0.83, so exact projection is better there by roughly 1.2 to 1.4 times.

key_findings.claim: A direction that is greedily superior at every visited iterate can still yield a much worse trajectory than GD, even when both directions receive exact line search on the true quadratic.
key_findings.evidence: For a 100-by-100 quadratic with spectrum (1,...,1,1000), the greedy policy compares exact-line-search GD and polar decreases and selects the polar direction at every iteration, yet the independent GD trajectory reduces objective much faster across 100 random starts. Appendix G shows the same ordering in gradient norm and distance to the minimizer.

anchors.section: Appendix G, exact line search and Figure 16

key_findings.claim: The analyzed algorithms omit several coupled components of the practical Muon recipe, so the paper is a diagnostic counterexample study rather than an explanation of LLM-training performance.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A's reference implementation uses variable learning rate, momentum scheduled from 0.85 to 0.95, weight decay, global normalization, rectangular correction, five bfloat16 PolarExpress polynomials, and AdamW for nonmatrix parameters. The main exact-polar analyses and controlled quadratics remove most of these components and use deterministic full gradients.

anchors.section: Appendix A-B, PolarExpress and momentum variants

key_findings.claim: The finite-budget spectrum experiment uses outcome-aware hyperparameter selection and one constructed quadratic per spectrum family, so its binary win rates are descriptive rather than an unbiased estimate over a problem distribution.
key_findings.evidence: For each method the learning rate in {0.1,0.01,0.001} is selected using the smallest loss achieved through the full T=500 horizon. The 100 repetitions vary W0 for a fixed constructed X and planted W-star rather than resampling the Hessian family, and no compute or wall-clock cost is matched.

anchors.section: Appendix D.1-D.2, Problem family and learning-rate selection

method.core_idea: Use exactly solvable matrix quadratics to separate four often-conflated aspects of Muon: discrete fixed-step polar dynamics, Hessian spectral shape, polar approximation error, and locally optimal one-step decrease.
method.mechanism: The isotropic loss diagonalizes the exact-polar update into scalar sign recurrences, exposing lattice confinement and residual stationarity. Prescribed-spectrum least-squares Hessians then hold condition number fixed while varying eigenvalue shape. An additive Gaussian perturbation of scalar sign dynamics isolates reachability, actual five-step Newton-Schulz provides a structured inexactness check, and an exact-line-search greedy selector tests whether local polar advantage predicts a separate full trajectory.
assumptions: The core nonconvergence result uses deterministic full gradients, an exact polar factor, a fixed positive step, and square matrix parameters; singular vectors decouple exactly on the isotropic quadratic.
The stationarity bound assumes Frobenius c-smoothness, a lower-bounded loss, and exact spectral-norm linear-minimization-oracle updates.
The O(1/square-root-of-ε) discussion assumes generic lattice misalignment or neighborhood-scale reachability; exact hits under specially aligned α and W0 are exceptions.

Controlled-spectrum experiments use noiseless 100-by-100 least squares, one prescribed Hessian per family, 100 random initializations, a 500-step budget, and hindsight selection among three learning rates.

The noisy-sign theorem assumes independent, centered Gaussian perturbations across time; actual Newton-Schulz errors are state-dependent, biased by polynomial shape, globally normalized across singular values, and temporally coupled.
The one-step counterexample uses exact line search and compares independent optimizer trajectories, not identical future iterates after one counterfactual step.
No theorem transfers the quadratic mechanisms quantitatively to stochastic neural-network or language-model training.

techniques.role: Diagonalizes the exact-polar update on the isotropic quadratic into independent scalar sign recurrences.
Tracks the additive subgroup s0+αZ to distinguish stationarity floors from actual convergence to the minimizer.
Connects the discrete two-cycle to the O(α) gradient and O(α²) loss residuals in standard smoothness bounds.
Keeps eigenvalue endpoints and condition number fixed while changing the full Hessian spectral distribution.
Models projection error as Gaussian perturbations and proves almost-sure hitting by drift plus repeated uniform attempts.
Uses deterministic shadowing for σ→0 and Gaussian anti-concentration for σ→infinity to bound finite-horizon hitting.
Tests whether the implemented Newton-Schulz-style approximation improves finite-budget loss relative to exact projection.
Selects the locally better of Euclidean and polar directions at each iterate to falsify one-step-to-trajectory inference.

evaluations.setting: Page 5, Section 3.1 and page 17, Appendix C: exact-polar constant-step optimization of L(W)=one-half times squared Frobenius norm, plus a generic c-smooth-loss descent calculation.
evaluations.metric: Minimizer reachability, limiting cycle scale, and minimum nuclear gradient norm over T steps.
evaluations.result: Generic singular values enter nonzero two-cycles; the theorem-level bound is (L(W0)-L*)/(Tα)+cdα/2 and therefore retains an O(α) stationarity floor.
evaluations.baseline: The global minimizer W=0 and the vanishing-step requirement needed to remove the residual.

evaluations.setting: Page 6, Section 3.2: isotropic strongly convex quadratic under fixed exact-polar steps.
evaluations.metric: Iteration scaling to loss at most ε.
evaluations.result: Choosing α=O(square-root-of-ε) gives Θ(1/square-root-of-ε) steps before the ε-scale cycle, subject to generic reachability qualifications.
evaluations.baseline: GD reaches this isotropic optimum in one step at learning rate 1 and has O(log(1/ε)) dependence on general smooth strongly convex objectives.

evaluations.setting: Pages 6-7, Section 3.3 and Table 1; pages 18-19, Appendix D.1-D.4 and Table 3: seven 100-dimensional noiseless least-squares spectra with κ=10,000, T=500, 100 random initializations, and best-of-{0.1,0.01,0.001} learning rates.
evaluations.metric: Muon win rate at T/10, T/2, and T and mean best-GD-loss divided by best-Muon-loss.
evaluations.result: Final win rates are 1 for min-spiked, U-shaped, and geometric-decay-to-max and 0 for four other families; final ratios include 949±620, 2.48±0.018, and 78.0±0.3 on the favorable families, versus at most 0.02 on four unfavorable ones.
evaluations.baseline: Exact-projection, no-momentum Muon versus standard GD, each tuned separately using the full horizon.

evaluations.setting: Pages 21-22, Appendix D.6, Figures 10-13 and Tables 4-7: cosine-annealed learning rates and Muon variants with or without momentum and Newton-Schulz projection.
evaluations.metric: Best-loss win rate versus GD at T/10, T/2, and T.
evaluations.result: The dominant spectrum ranking persists; linear-decay-to-max is the only notable borderline case, with final win rates between 0 and 0.31 across variants.
evaluations.baseline: Best constant-step GD compared with four vanishing-step Muon variants.

evaluations.setting: Pages 25-27, Appendix D.7, Figures 14-15: gradient-conditioning diagnostics on the controlled spectra.
evaluations.metric: Gradient condition number along GD and corresponding loss-trajectory ordering.
evaluations.result: Uniform and geometric-decay-to-max both fall from about 10^8 to 10^7 in gradient conditioning, but Muon wins only on the geometric spectrum.
evaluations.baseline: A proposed explanation based on gradient conditioning alone.

evaluations.setting: Pages 28-32, Appendix E, Propositions E.1-E.2: one-dimensional Gaussian-perturbed sign dynamics whose deterministic lattice misses [−ε,ε] by margin Δ.
evaluations.metric: Almost-sure hitting and fixed-horizon tail probability P(Tε(σ)>N).
evaluations.result: Every σ>0 hits almost surely, while for every fixed N the miss probability tends to 1 as σ tends to either 0 or infinity.
evaluations.baseline: At σ=0 the off-grid deterministic recurrence has infinite hitting time.

evaluations.setting: Page 10, Figure 4 and page 32, Appendix F.1: α=0.1, ε=0.02, s0=1.026, σ on a log grid from 0.001 to 10, 10,000 runs, and a 1,000-step cap.
evaluations.metric: Median capped ε-hitting time and 2.5th-97.5th empirical percentiles.
evaluations.result: Median time is nonmonotone and has an intermediate empirical sweet spot; the figure does not tabulate an optimal σ or uncertainty over experimental seeds.
evaluations.baseline: The unreachable noiseless recurrence and its first zero-crossing time |s0|/α.

evaluations.setting: Pages 9-10, Section 4.3 and Table 2; page 32, Appendix F.2 and Table 8: actual Newton-Schulz versus exact projection on the same seven controlled spectra, no momentum, T=500.
evaluations.metric: Win rate and exact-best-loss divided by Newton-Schulz-best-loss.
evaluations.result: Final win rates favor approximation only for max-spiked (0.92) and min-spiked (0.94); the final ratio is 33.18±8.96 for min-spiked but 0.71-0.83 on five families where approximation loses.
evaluations.baseline: Exact polar projection with the same learning-rate search and no momentum.

evaluations.setting: Pages 10-11, Section 5 and Figure 5; page 33, Appendix G and Figure 16: 100-by-100 quadratic with eigenvalues (1,...,1,1000), exact line search, and 100 Gaussian initializations.
evaluations.metric: Objective gap, Frobenius gradient norm, distance to W-star, and which direction the greedy policy selects.
evaluations.result: The greedy policy selects polar at every step yet is visibly much slower than GD on all three trajectory metrics; no numerical summary table is provided.

limitations: [Author-stated, pages 7 and 11] The spectra favorable to Muon only resemble reported neural-network Hessians qualitatively; the authors explicitly say no definitive neural-network conclusion follows.

[Author-stated, pages 8-9] Independent Gaussian sign noise is an isolating toy model, not Newton-Schulz error, whose singular-value errors are jointly normalized and correlated across indices and time.
[Author-stated, page 11] The paper presents quadratics as filters on universal explanations and leaves a full theory of spectral structure and approximation profiles open.
[Reviewer-inferred] All core evaluations are deterministic square quadratics of size 100; there are no stochastic gradients, nonquadratic networks, language-model losses, or scale studies.

[Reviewer-inferred] The spectrum study resamples initial conditions but appears to retain one constructed objective per family, so it does not estimate variance across Hessians with the same spectral law.

[Reviewer-inferred] Learning rates are chosen by the best loss observed through the full 500-step horizon, an oracle selection protocol that can favor methods differently and is not an online tuning rule.
[Reviewer-inferred] Iterations are not matched for matrix-multiplication, SVD, wall-clock, memory, or tuning cost; exact projection is computationally unlike practical Muon.
[Reviewer-inferred] The dramatic min-spiked final ratio, 949±620, is imprecise, and the paper reports no independent problem seeds or correction for the many spectrum-time-variant comparisons.
[Reviewer-inferred] The fixed-step O(1/square-root-of-ε) language is not universal over step sizes and initializations because exact lattice alignment can hit the optimum finitely.
[Reviewer-inferred] Almost-sure eventual hitting under nonzero noise gives no finite expectation, usable high-probability runtime, or stationary-loss guarantee.

[Reviewer-inferred] The practical reference recipe contains schedules, weight decay, rectangular scaling, mixed AdamW parameters, bfloat16 polynomial arithmetic, and momentum that the central theorems do not jointly model.
failure_modes: Exact polar updates with a nonvanishing step can oscillate forever near, but not at, a minimizer whenever one or more initial singular-value lattices miss zero.
Pre-projection momentum preserves fixed-magnitude projected displacements and therefore cannot by itself escape the scalar lattice trap.
A vanishing schedule can remove the asymptotic trap too late to improve a finite budget after GD has already converged.
Approximation that is too weak behaves nearly deterministically and may retain long lattice-like transients; approximation that is too strong overshoots a narrow target through diffusion.
Newton-Schulz approximation can worsen finite-time loss even when its polar error is small: it loses to exact projection on five of seven tested spectral families at T.
Condition-number-based optimizer selection can fail because Hessians with identical endpoints and κ have opposite Muon-GD rankings.
One-step polar improvement can repeatedly choose a globally inferior path because each choice changes the future gradient and curvature geometry.

Post-projection momentum may escape the lattice but is outside default Muon and has distinct empirical behavior, so it cannot be used to rescue claims about the implemented algorithm without a separate analysis.
Results may reverse under stochastic gradients, rectangular layers, learned features, or coupled optimizer components not represented by the simple quadratics.
reusable_insights: For normalized or sign-like optimizers, analyze the additive group generated by step sizes before interpreting a stationarity bound as minimizer convergence.
Separate reachability, asymptotic error floor, hitting-time distribution, and expected runtime; they are different properties even in one dimension.
Hold spectral endpoints fixed and vary the eigenvalue distribution when testing any explanation based only on condition number.
Approximation error can be a structured dynamical intervention rather than a monotone numerical-accuracy penalty, so profile its bias, tails, and state dependence.
A same-iterate one-step comparison is not sufficient for optimizer selection; follow the induced trajectories or prove an invariant that links local choices to future geometry.

Audit practical optimizer definitions component by component—projection placement, momentum placement, schedule, scaling, weight decay, and parameter partition—before transferring an idealized theorem.
Extreme-regime theorems can motivate but do not establish an interior optimum; explicitly distinguish mathematical endpoints from simulation-observed sweet spots.
open_questions: Which state-dependent properties of real Newton-Schulz or PolarExpress error determine whether it helps a given spectrum?
Can one derive finite expected or high-probability hitting-time bounds, not only almost-sure reachability, for noisy polar dynamics?
What spectral statistics beyond κ predict the crossover between Euclidean and polar updates across resampled objectives and neural-network checkpoints?
Can a trajectory-level potential characterize when repeated one-step spectral advantages compound rather than redirect the optimizer onto a slow path?
How do stochastic-gradient noise and approximation error interact—constructively or destructively—near fixed-step cycles?
Do rectangular layers, low-rank gradients, weight decay, and mixed AdamW parameters preserve or eliminate the lattice mechanisms?
Can a practical switching rule use polar updates early and GD-like refinement late without horizon-aware tuning?
How do compute-matched results change when exact SVD, five polynomial steps, GD, and AdamW are compared at equal wall-clock and tuning budget?

competitive_landscape.title: A Note on the Convergence of Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: Li and Hong analyze exact-polar Muon as matrix normalized/steepest descent and establish stationarity-style convergence implications. The target paper exposes what a fixed-step stationarity residual does not give on a strongly convex objective: generic minimizer reachability, and it adds explicit two-cycles and trajectory counterexamples.

competitive_landscape.title: Beyond the Ideal: Analyzing the Inexact Muon Update
competitive_landscape.difference: Shulgin et al. model an inexact linear minimization oracle by an additive norm error and derive bounds whose constants degrade with error, plus learning-rate/momentum coupling and NanoGPT experiments. The target instead gives a constructive stochastic perturbation mechanism and spectrum-dependent Newton-Schulz cases where inexactness helps, while offering no comparable neural experiment or general convergence bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Isotropic Curvature Model for Understanding Deep Learning Optimization: Is Gradient Orthogonalization Optimal?
competitive_landscape.difference: Su solves an isotropic-curvature one-iteration model and identifies when homogenizing or fully orthogonalizing a gradient spectrum is locally optimal. The target shows that even exact line search on the true quadratic can select the polar direction at every visited point while yielding a slower end-to-end trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: When do spectral gradient updates help in deep learning?
competitive_landscape.difference: Davis and Drusvyatskiy give a layerwise local-decrease condition comparing gradient nuclear-to-Frobenius ratio with activation stable rank and validate it in synthetic regression and NanoGPT. The target does not dispute the local condition; it demonstrates that persistent local superiority alone cannot certify a faster trajectory.

competitive_landscape.title: Preconditioning Benefits of Spectral Orthogonalization in Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: Ma et al. prove condition-number-independent linear convergence for simplified Muon on matrix factorization and linear-transformer in-context learning using decoupled spectral dynamics and vanishing schedules. The target studies generic prescribed quadratics and shows that κ alone does not predict finite-budget ranking; it is a negative boundary on extrapolating those structured positive cases.

competitive_landscape.title: Convergence of Muon with Newton-Schulz
competitive_landscape.difference: Kim and Oh prove nonconvex nuclear-norm stationarity for finite-step Newton-Schulz Muon, with an approximation factor tending to one doubly exponentially in the number of polynomial steps. The target stresses that stationarity with fixed-step residuals need not imply minimizer convergence and that smaller approximation error need not monotonically improve finite-time reachability.

competitive_landscape.title: The Spectral Dynamics and Noise Geometry of Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: Beneventano et al. derive continuous-time spectral flattening under alignment assumptions and show Muon wins on small NanoGPT but loses on a small ViT. The target's earlier discrete-time contribution is lattice reachability, prescribed-Hessian ranking flips, and a one-step trajectory counterexample rather than an implicit-bias account.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Understanding the Power and Limits of the Muon Optimizer: A River-Valley Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Shen et al. independently develop a trajectory theory in which Muon moves quickly along an information-bearing river early but overshoots and oscillates near the target, including an exactly solvable quadratic and a GD-switching proposal. This substantially overlaps the target's warning about late fixed-step polar dynamics, while adding structured matrix sensing and preliminary language-model switching evidence; the target remains earlier and uniquely emphasizes constructive approximation error and greedy one-step failure.

competitive_landscape.title: On MUON optimization: From non-convergence to an error analysis with Polar Express and the Newton-Schulz polynomial from implementations
competitive_landscape.relationship: later closest nonconvergence and implementation-error analysis
competitive_landscape.difference: Do, Dereich, and Jentzen prove nonconvergence for generalized Newton-Schulz Muon itself on simple stochastic quadratics for almost every mini-batch size and give error rates in steps and batch size, covering original and PolarExpress polynomials. It narrows any broad priority claim about practical-Muon nonconvergence: the target predates it but proves only exact-polar lattice confinement, then separately studies a toy noise model and finite Newton-Schulz experiments.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim that simple strongly convex quadratics invalidate three common abstractions: fixed-step exact Muon need not reach the minimizer, approximation error can constructively improve reachability and speed, and one-step polar superiority need not yield faster end-to-end optimization; they also claim full spectral shape matters beyond condition number.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact scalar reduction gives a transparent lattice counterexample; seven matched-κ spectra flip the finite-budget ranking; Propositions E.1-E.2 and Figure 4 establish constructive perturbation reachability and an empirical interior regime; Table 8 shows actual approximation can help or hurt; and the exact-line-search quadratic forces the greedy policy to choose polar at every step while losing globally.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the combination of a clean discrete-time reachability audit, an explicit constructive-inexactness counterexample, a matched-condition-number spectrum-shape panel, and a local-to-global trajectory falsification. It is not the first convergence, inexact-LMO, condition-independent structured-case, or one-step Muon analysis. Later 2026 river-valley and generalized-Newton-Schulz papers substantially overlap the nonconvergence/overshoot story and extend it toward structured sensing or the implemented polynomial, so novelty should be stated narrowly as an early quadratic diagnostic synthesis rather than a general theory of Muon or its LLM advantage.

reviewer_notes: Read all 33 extracted pages, including practical pseudocode, all momentum variants, the stationarity proof, controlled-spectrum construction and Tables 3-7, gradient-conditioning diagnostics, both noisy-sign proofs, exact-versus-Newton-Schulz Table 8, and exact-line-search formulas/plots. The mathematical lattice and Markov-chain claims are high confidence. Interpret 'steps must vanish' as a requirement for generic convergence guarantees, not for every specially aligned run, and interpret O(1/square-root-of-ε) as the generic neighborhood-scale construction rather than a universal instance-wise lower bound. The competitor panel was independently checked against current primary arXiv records and relevant PDFs on 2026-08-23; it includes post-target 2026 results so the novelty statement reflects the current, not submission-time, landscape.
